/itineraryStops/3/description.source_en:
⟦G0⟧ — opened 1905 as Korea's first permanent traditional market — sits in Jongno-gu about 10 minutes east of Bukchon and is the city's most-photographed streetfood alley, made world-famous by Anthony Bourdain's 'Parts Unknown' Seoul episode and again by Netflix's 'Street Food: Asia.' 

The covered alley layout puts dozens of cheek-by-jowl vendors specializing in Seoul's signature snacks: **bindaetteok** (mung-bean pancakes ground fresh on stone mills, fried golden-crisp in pork-lard pans — the market's most iconic dish, 5,000-7,000 KRW per pancake); **mayak gimbap** (literally 'drug gimbap' — bite-sized seaweed-rice rolls dipped in mustard-soy sauce, named for their addictive quality, 3,000-5,000 KRW per plate); **yukhoe** (Korean-style raw beef tartare with pear and egg yolk — Cham Sundae stall #18 is the famous purveyor); **sundae** (Korean blood sausage); **tteokbokki** (spicy rice cakes); **kalguksu** (handmade knife-cut noodle soup); **soondae-guk** and **gopchang-jeongol** (offal stew). 

Beyond the food alley: the market's cloth-and-textile district on the second floor (silks, Korean wedding hanbok fabrics) is a separate Korea-only specialty. Cruise passengers typically eat at sit-down counters where each vendor has 5-10 stools — pay-as-you-order, mostly cash, English menu boards now available at most stalls. 

Critical: most vendors are CASH-ONLY. Bring 10,000-20,000 KRW per person. Note: peak lunch crowds 12:00-14:00 mean wait times — the 13:45 arrival is timed for the easing-off post-peak hour.

/itineraryStops/4/highlights/1.source_en: Ssamzigil — 4-story spiral cultural complex with 70+ shops, galleries, cafes

/itineraryStops/4/highlights/2.source_en: Traditional teahouses (jeontongchatjip): Mokyeon, Suyeonsanbang for classical tea ceremony

/itineraryStops/4/highlights/3.source_en: Hanji (mulberry paper) workshops with hands-on folding/stamping demos

/itineraryStops/4/highlights/4.source_en: Ceramic galleries: Goryeo celadon and Joseon white porcelain

/itineraryStops/4/highlights/5.source_en: Balwoo Gongyang — Korea's only Michelin-starred Buddhist temple cuisine restaurant nearby

/itineraryStops/4/highlights/7.source_en: **Pedestrian-only on Saturdays + Sundays** (vehicles cleared) — best photo days; weekday vehicle-share zone has narrower walking margins

/itineraryStops/4/highlights/8.source_en: **⟦G0⟧ 5-min walk south** — head temple of Jogye Order (Korea's largest Buddhist denomination); FREE admission, the only major traditional temple in central Seoul; Daeungjeon = largest temple building in Seoul; 500-year-old Baeksong (Natural Monument No. 9)

/itineraryStops/4/smartNotes/tip.source_en: **Best souvenirs**: hanji paper crafts, traditional ink stamps (dojang), small ceramics, Korean knot-tying kits, traditional tea sampler boxes. Skip if you don't shop — the street's appeal is browse-and-buy. Ssamzigil rooftop terrace has photo-worthy city views and is free entry. Balwoo Gongyang Michelin temple cuisine requires advance reservation. Visit on Saturday or Sunday when the street is fully pedestrian (no cars).

/itineraryStops/4/smartNotes/facilities.source_en: Cafes, teahouses, restaurants, galleries throughout. Tourist Information Center at Anguk Station Exit 6. Tax refund counters at major souvenir shops. ATMs at Anguk Station and Jongno 3-ga Station.

/itineraryStops/4/whyOnRoute.source_en: ⟦G0⟧ closes the Seoul highlights loop with the city's strongest traditional-crafts shopping experience — the natural complement to Bukchon's residential hanok and Gwangjang's working-class food culture. Picked over the Dongdaemun area (larger but fashion-and-modern-shopping focused) because ⟦G0⟧'s craft-and-tea concentration is unmatched in Seoul and aligns with the cruise-passenger souvenir-purchase window. For cruise guests, ⟦G0⟧ is the day's primary souvenir-purchase window — Korean ceramics + hanji paper + tea + traditional crafts are concentrated in this single 700-m pedestrian street, eliminating the need for fragmented shopping across multiple Seoul districts.

/itineraryStops/4/convenience/parking.source_en: Limited; walking from Bukchon (5 min) or Jongno 3-ga subway access

/itineraryStops/4/convenience/restroom.source_en: Ssamzigil + Tourist Information Center at Anguk Station Exit 6
